To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the closed loop behaviour (in terms of the buffer occupancy distribution) of a buffer fed by LRD traffic under adaptive window control is different from the open loop behaviour (in that the buffer occupancy distribution has a lighter tail) and that the closed loop buffer behaviour is sensitive to the file size (and hence the traffic) distribution.
the buffer behaviour is sensitive to the file size distributions, and that the buffer occupancy process is not always long range dependent, even when the file sizes are heavy tailed.
(i) under AWP-controlled traffic, the buffer occupancy is not necessarily heavy tailed; and (ii) the buffer occupancy is sensitive to the file size distributions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What is the nature of the traffic into the Internet link buffers?
the analysis and control of the Internet link buffers, and the results presented are useful in the design of Internet routers.
the following questions: (i) How does the window size evolution under an adaptive window protocol affect the traffic into the buffer?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the buffer behaviour of the Internet is sensitive not only to the distribution of packet inter-arrival times but also to the file size distributions.

the buffer behaviour is sensitive to the window protocol and the file size distributions, and the sensitivity is such that the closed loop behaviour can be significantly different from the open loop behaviour.

the performance of TCP-controlled transfer of finite volume files is much better than what is predicted by open loop analysis, and the file size (and hence the application type) distribution plays an important role in this performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the closed loop behaviour under AWP-controlled file transfer can be quite different from the open loop analysis, and that the closed loop analysis can also provide a more accurate prediction of the buffer behaviour than an open loop analysis.

the buffer occupancy under AWP-controlled transfers of Pareto-distribution files is sensitive to the file size distributions, and the buffer occupancy process can be finite even though the traffic is LRD.

we provide a framework for analysing the link buffer behaviour for AWP-controlled transfer with general file size distributions, and that this framework provides new insights into the buffer behaviour under TCP.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the closed loop control under AWP can be used to improve buffer performance for a given distribution of file sizes and a given AWP.

the buffer behaviour of an adaptive window protocol-controlled link buffer is more sensitive to the distributional properties of file sizes than to the Hurst parameters of the traffic into the buffer.
the buffer occupancy process is not a stationary process and hence the open loop analysis is not applicable to this problem.
